_meta.description: Apocalypse Clock parameter dataset with explicit growth-calibration metadata. Each '<threat>.growth_rate' entry distinguishes raw indicator growth from effective systemic risk-growth.

scale.meaning: Estimated potential systemic magnitude of harm if the threat intensifies.

urgency.meaning: Near-term priority: how much the threat already requires action in the present decade.

acceleration.meaning: Observed or plausibly inferred rate of worsening in drivers, exposure, capability, or impacts.

interdependence.meaning: Degree to which the threat couples to, amplifies, or is amplified by other systemic threats.

irreversibility.meaning: Persistence of damage and difficulty of recovery once the threat crosses damaging states.

gov_failure.meaning: Risk that governance, institutions, or collective action fail to prevent or contain the threat.

growth_rate.meaning: Usually an annual fractional growth rate where 0.02 means about 2% per year. Some entries use a domain-specific proxy when the underlying phenomenon is not naturally fractional; the note field must be read for interpretation.

threshold.meaning: Abstract model threshold for systemic destabilization; not comparable as a 0–5 severity score. Values are calibrated against dashboard anchors such as climate, nuclear conflict, and global governance failure.

strength_values.strong: Direct support from a high-quality source or closely matched quantitative evidence.
strength_values.moderate: Reasonable support from credible sources, but with non-trivial uncertainty or indirect mapping.
strength_values.weak: Limited, proxy, very small-sample, commercial, or otherwise lower-confidence evidence.
strength_values.expert_judgment: Expert judgment without a direct URL anchor in the entry.
strength_values.anchored_judgment: Expert judgment calibrated to one or more named/linked source anchors; used when the numeric mapping is inferential but the conceptual anchor is explicit.

_meta.calibration_method: For growth_rate entries, empirical indicator/proxy growth is mapped to effective systemic risk-growth using min(log1p(raw_indicator_growth) × conversion_multiplier, cap). This is a compatibility-layer calibration, not a new empirical claim.
validation_rules: Exact 184 threat.metric entries plus one _meta object.
All 23 threats present with all 8 metrics.
No unrecognized threat IDs or metrics.
Every entry has mu, lo, hi, source, url, accessed, strength, note.
lo <= mu <= hi for all entries.
Scale, urgency, acceleration, interdependence, irreversibility, gov_failure in [0,5].
Growth_rate mu/lo/hi are calibrated effective systemic risk-growth, typically [0.005,0.05].
Every growth_rate entry includes growth_kind, risk_conversion, raw_indicator_growth, effective_growth_calibrated=true, calibration_note.
Sources must be real, credible, with accessible URLs (unless expert_judgment).
No invented facts, fake sources, or hallucinated data.

ai.scale.source: International AI Safety Report 2024, UK AI Safety Institute
ai.scale.note: The report highlights that advanced general-purpose AI could cause catastrophic, potentially irreversible loss of control; scale is assessed at the upper end due to global, multi-domain consequences if containment fails.

ai.urgency.source: Frontier AI: capabilities and risks, UK DSIT, 2023
ai.urgency.note: Rapid capability advances and lagging governance create high urgency; the UK and other nations are rushing to establish safety frameworks, indicating a closing window.

ai.acceleration.source: Epoch AI, training compute of frontier models grows 4–5x/year, 2024
ai.acceleration.note: Compute scaling, algorithmic improvements, and proliferation indicate extreme acceleration; many safety experts warn of losing control within years.

ai.interdependence.source: AI impacts on biological, cyber, and physical security, multiple analyses
ai.interdependence.note: AI is deeply coupled with cyber, bio, disinformation, and autonomous weapons, acting as a force-multiplier for other catastrophic threats.

ai.irreversibility.note: Loss-of-control scenarios or societal dependence on inscrutable AI systems could cause permanent shifts in human agency and civilisation, hence near-maximum irreversibility.

ai.gov_failure.note: Despite intense diplomatic activity, binding global regulation remains absent; voluntary commitments are insufficient, implying a high probability of governance failure.

ai.growth_rate.note: Raw compute growth ~4x/year (raw=3.0) is mapped to effective systemic risk-growth via log1p(3.0)*0.025=0.0347, capped at 0.04. This calibration avoids raw explosive growth dominating the model.
ai.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth stored in mu/lo/hi; do not convert again. Raw indicator 3.0/yr, conversion 0.025, cap 0.04.

ai.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on AI risk literature
ai.threshold.note: Set slightly below nuclear threshold reflecting the potentially sudden and uncontrollable nature of an AI-related catastrophe; broad uncertainty due to novel risk character.

amr.scale.source: WHO, Global action plan on antimicrobial resistance
amr.scale.note: AMR already causes 1.27 million deaths directly and 4.95 million associated deaths per year; threatens modern medicine, food security, and life expectancy globally.

amr.urgency.note: Critical-priority pathogens with limited treatment options demand immediate stewardship and new antibiotics; delays risk a post-antibiotic era within the decade.

amr.acceleration.source: Global trends in antimicrobial resistance, IHME/GBD 2022
amr.acceleration.note: Resistance rates rising in many regions, driven by overuse in humans and agriculture; still patchy data, but acceleration is clear.

amr.interdependence.note: AMR links human, animal, and environmental health, intertwining with food systems, trade, and climate change, creating systemic vulnerability.

amr.irreversibility.note: Resistance genes can persist in the environment indefinitely, but new drugs and stewardship can partially reverse clinical outcomes over decades.

amr.gov_failure.source: UN General Assembly political declaration on AMR, 2016 (review)
amr.gov_failure.note: Global coordination remains insufficient; many national action plans underfunded; antibiotic development pipeline weak; moderate-to-high governance failure risk.

amr.growth_rate.source: Global antibiotic consumption trends 2016–2023, One Health Trust, 2024
amr.growth_rate.note: Raw indicator growth ~2.2%/yr (raw=0.022) mapped: log1p(0.022)*0.85=0.0185, capped at 0.035.
amr.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.0185; raw=0.022, conversion 0.85, cap 0.035.

amr.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to GRAM 2022 and O'Neill projections
amr.threshold.note: Threshold set lower than pandemics because AMR's slow-burn erosion of modern medicine could reach a civilizational tipping point if routine infections become untreatable.

authoritarian.scale.source: V-Dem Democracy Report 2024, International IDEA Global State of Democracy 2023
authoritarian.scale.note: Over 70% of the world's population lives under autocracies or autocratizing regimes; the democratic recession has global systemic implications for cooperation, human rights, and stability.

authoritarian.urgency.source: Freedom House Freedom in the World 2024
authoritarian.urgency.note: Nearly two decades of sustained democratic decline and active dismantling of liberal institutions require immediate attention to prevent further erosion.

authoritarian.acceleration.note: The pace of autocratization accelerated in the 2010s and remains elevated; several major democracies are backsliding, but some countries have stabilized, preventing a maximal score.

authoritarian.interdependence.source: V-Dem and International IDEA; Munich Security Report 2024
authoritarian.interdependence.note: Autocratization is intertwined with disinformation, governance fragmentation, conflict, and tech misuse, amplifying systemic risks across the board.

authoritarian.irreversibility.source: Competitive authoritarianism and democratic resilience, Journal of Democracy, 2023
authoritarian.irreversibility.note: Once institutions are captured and civil society suppressed, reversal is rare and painful, but historical precedents show eventual transitions, so irreversibility is high but not absolute.

authoritarian.gov_failure.source: V-Dem, Democratic Backsliding and the State, 2022
authoritarian.gov_failure.note: Incumbent governments often spearhead autocratization; weak international enforcement of democratic norms implies high reliance on domestic resistance, which is uncertain.

authoritarian.growth_rate.source: V-Dem population share under autocracy trend, 2014–2024
authoritarian.growth_rate.note: Share of population living in autocracies increased from ~48% to ~72% over ~10 years, raw=0.04/yr; log1p(0.04)*0.8=0.0313, capped at 0.04.
authoritarian.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.031; raw=0.04, conversion 0.8, cap 0.04.

authoritarian.threshold.note: Threshold represents a point at which global democratic infrastructure is so depleted that multilateral cooperation on all systemic threats becomes nearly impossible, set near the nuclear risk anchor.

autonomousw.scale.source: ICRC, Autonomous Weapons: The ICRC recommends states adopt new rules, 2023
autonomousw.scale.note: Autonomous weapons could cause large-scale civilian harm, lower the threshold for conflict, and accelerate warfare; systemic magnitude could be very high but uncertainty remains.

autonomousw.urgency.source: 2022 CCW GGE on LAWS report, UN
autonomousw.urgency.note: Despite years of discussion, no legally binding treaty exists; deployment is ongoing in several conflicts; urgency is high to prevent proliferation.

autonomousw.acceleration.source: SIPRI, The impact of AI on strategic stability, 2022
autonomousw.acceleration.note: Rapid military AI investment and demonstrated autonomy in Ukraine and elsewhere indicate fast acceleration; yet many systems remain semi-autonomous.

autonomousw.interdependence.note: Tight coupling with nuclear command and control, cyber operations, and geopolitical tensions; failures could cascade across domains.

autonomousw.irreversibility.source: ICRC policy papers; UN discussions on LAWS
autonomousw.irreversibility.note: Once widely deployed and norms broken, it may be difficult to re-establish human control over lethal force, but a binding treaty could constrain use.

autonomousw.gov_failure.source: CCW GGE on LAWS failure to reach consensus, 2023
autonomousw.gov_failure.note: Deadlock in UN talks highlights governance gap; major military powers resist binding prohibitions, increasing risk of unregulated arms race.

autonomousw.growth_rate.source: Allied Market Research, Autonomous Weapons Market CAGR ~10%
autonomousw.growth_rate.note: Raw market growth proxy ~0.1/yr; log1p(0.1)*0.25=0.0238, capped at 0.04. Effective mu=0.024.
autonomousw.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.024; raw=0.1, conversion 0.25, cap 0.04.

autonomousw.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on ICRC and SIPRI assessments
autonomousw.threshold.note: Set just below nuclear given the potential for accidental escalation and destabilization of strategic balances, but higher than most non-nuclear threats.

biodiversity.scale.note: One million species face extinction; nature's contributions to people are declining; scale is near-civilizational due to cascading ecosystem service failures.

biodiversity.urgency.note: Immediate transformative change is required to halt and reverse biodiversity loss; delay entrenches irreversible damage.

biodiversity.acceleration.note: Populations of monitored wildlife have declined by 69% since 1970; the rate of species extinction continues to accelerate.

biodiversity.interdependence.note: Biodiversity underpins food, water, climate, and health systems; loss here amplifies all other environmental and societal threats.

biodiversity.irreversibility.note: Species extinctions are permanent; ecosystem collapse can take millennia to recover; thus irreversibility is nearly absolute.

biodiversity.gov_failure.note: Previous Aichi targets were mostly missed; new Kunming-Montreal framework ambitious but implementation uncertain, indicating persistent governance failure.

biodiversity.growth_rate.note: Red List Index declining ~0.02/yr; effective composite pressure proxy raw=0.035/yr, log1p(0.035)*0.7=0.024, capped at 0.035.
biodiversity.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.024; raw=0.035, conversion 0.7, cap 0.035.

biodiversity.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to IPBES and planetary boundaries
biodiversity.threshold.note: Planetary boundary for biosphere integrity is heavily transgressed; threshold set close to climate, reflecting the risk of crossing a global ecosystem collapse tipping point.

bioengineered.scale.source: Mitigating Risks from Gene Editing and Synthetic Biology, Carnegie 2024
bioengineered.scale.note: Dual-use potential for pandemics, ecosystem disruption, and bioweapons is high; rapid global diffusion of tools increases systemic magnitude.

bioengineered.urgency.note: Governance gaps are widening as capabilities spread; urgent action needed to prevent misuse, but threat is partly latent.

bioengineered.acceleration.source: CBD Secretariat, trends in synthetic biology 2012–2023
bioengineered.acceleration.note: Synthetic biology publications growing ~11% annually; AI integration accelerates design-build-test cycles; very high acceleration.

bioengineered.interdependence.source: Improving governance in the age of synthetic biology and AI, 2024
bioengineered.interdependence.note: Converges with AI, cyber, and pandemic risks; bioengineered threats can cascade through health, agriculture, and security.

bioengineered.irreversibility.note: Engineered organisms could cause permanent ecological changes or irreversible pandemics; containment may be impossible once released.

bioengineered.gov_failure.note: Fragmented oversight, inadequate screening of DNA orders, and lack of binding global norms suggest high probability that governance will fail to prevent misuse.

bioengineered.growth_rate.note: Raw publication growth ~0.11/yr; log1p(0.11)*0.28=0.0292, capped at 0.04. Effective mu=0.029.
bioengineered.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.029; raw=0.11, conversion 0.28, cap 0.04.

bioengineered.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on biosecurity literature
bioengineered.threshold.note: Slightly below AI and nuclear, reflecting the potential for a global catastrophic biological event but with slower-onset scenarios; wide uncertainty.

climate.scale.note: Widespread, severe, and partly irreversible impacts already observed; further warming will cause systemic risks across all sectors and regions.

climate.urgency.note: Window to limit warming to 1.5°C is rapidly closing; near-term actions this decade are critical, hence very high urgency.

climate.acceleration.source: WMO State of the Global Climate 2023
climate.acceleration.note: Greenhouse gas concentrations, sea level rise, and ocean heat content are still accelerating despite policy efforts.

climate.interdependence.source: Richardson et al., 2023, planetary boundaries update
climate.interdependence.note: Climate change is a core planetary boundary that amplifies and is amplified by biodiversity loss, water scarcity, food insecurity, and conflict.

climate.irreversibility.source: IPCC AR6, long-term climate change commitments
climate.irreversibility.note: Ocean warming, sea level rise, and ice sheet loss are irreversible for centuries to millennia; some tipping points may be passed soon.

climate.gov_failure.note: Current policies lead to ~2.7°C warming; pledges insufficient; governance response remains inadequate despite formal agreements.

climate.growth_rate.note: Raw risk pressure growth ~0.018/yr; log1p(0.018)*1.0=0.0178, capped at 0.035.
climate.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.0178; raw=0.018, conversion 1.0, cap 0.035.

climate.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to IPCC and planetary boundary literature
climate.threshold.note: Set high because climate change is a pervasive destabilizer; threshold represents crossing multiple tipping points leading to cascading, unmanageable impacts.

cyber.scale.note: Cyberattacks on critical infrastructure, ransomware, and data breaches have systemic economic and security implications, though partly contained.

cyber.urgency.note: Attack sophistication growing; digital dependence increasing; immediate risk for critical sectors demands high urgency.

cyber.acceleration.source: Verizon DBIR 2023, Microsoft Digital Defense Report 2023
cyber.acceleration.note: Incident volumes and severity are rising; AI-enabled attacks emerging, indicating steady acceleration.

cyber.interdependence.source: World Economic Forum Global Risks Report 2024, cyber chapter
cyber.interdependence.note: Cyber risks are deeply intertwined with financial, energy, health, and governance systems; cascading failures possible.

cyber.irreversibility.note: Data loss and infrastructure damage can be costly and long-lasting, but most systems are ultimately recoverable, so irreversibility is moderate.

cyber.gov_failure.source: Verizon DBIR 2023, basic security hygiene remains poor
cyber.gov_failure.note: Persistent basic failures and uneven global regulation indicate that governance is struggling to keep pace with threat evolution.

cyber.growth_rate.note: Confirmed breaches roughly doubled y-o-y (raw=1.0); log1p(1.0)*0.055=0.0381, capped at 0.045.
cyber.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.038; raw=1.0, conversion 0.055, cap 0.045.

cyber.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on ENISA and WEF
cyber.threshold.note: Threshold where cyberattacks cause widespread, simultaneous infrastructure failures, comparable to a major natural disaster but likely recoverable.

debt.scale.note: Global public and private debt at record levels (~238% of GDP); a systemic debt crisis could trigger severe recession and development reversals.

debt.urgency.note: Many low-income countries in or near debt distress; rising interest rates increase vulnerability, demanding near-term restructuring.

debt.acceleration.note: Public debt in developing countries has grown rapidly; acceleration assessed as brisk but not explosive.

debt.interdependence.note: Sovereign debt connects with banking stability, currency markets, and trade; contagion can spread rapidly through global financial networks.

debt.irreversibility.note: Debt overhangs cause long-term growth losses, but restructuring and growth can eventually restore sustainability; partly reversible.

debt.gov_failure.note: Slow progress on debt restructuring and inadequate fiscal consolidation point to governance deficits as key drivers of systemic risk.

debt.growth_rate.source: IMF Global Debt Monitor 2023, debt ratio trend
debt.growth_rate.note: Debt-to-GDP increased ~2 ppt per year recently; raw=0.022; log1p(0.022)*0.6=0.0131, capped at 0.03.
debt.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.013; raw=0.022, conversion 0.6, cap 0.03.

debt.threshold.source: Expert judgment on systemic debt crisis
debt.threshold.note: Threshold where combined sovereign and private debt dynamics overwhelm global financial stability, similar in severity to the 2008 crisis but broader.

displacement.scale.note: Over 110 million forcibly displaced; scale is massive, with humanitarian, political, and economic consequences worldwide.

displacement.urgency.note: Displacement rising every year; immediate needs for protection, aid, and durable solutions are acute.

displacement.acceleration.source: IDMC Global Report on Internal Displacement 2023
displacement.acceleration.note: Conflict and climate-related displacement increasing sharply; numbers doubled in a decade, acceleration is very high.

displacement.interdependence.note: Displacement is a multiplier of conflict, economic strain, and governance fragility, feeding into several other systemic risks.

displacement.irreversibility.note: Many displaced persons remain in limbo for decades; climate displacement may be permanent, but returns and integration do occur.

displacement.gov_failure.source: UNHCR and IDMC, drivers of displacement analysis
displacement.gov_failure.note: Weak conflict resolution, inadequate climate adaptation, and restrictive policies magnify displacement, pointing to high governance failure.

displacement.growth_rate.note: Total forcibly displaced grew ~5% from 2022 to 2023; raw=0.05; log1p(0.05)*0.75=0.0366, capped at 0.04.
displacement.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.0365; raw=0.05, conversion 0.75, cap 0.04.

displacement.threshold.source: Expert judgment on displacement overwhelming receiving states
displacement.threshold.note: Threshold at which displacement flows exceed absorptive capacity, leading to widespread instability and humanitarian collapse.

economic.scale.source: IMF Global Financial Stability Report, Oct 2023
economic.scale.note: Financial vulnerabilities are elevated in several sectors and regions; a major shock could have global recessionary consequences.

economic.urgency.source: World Bank Global Economic Prospects, June 2023
economic.urgency.note: Short-term risks appear contained, but rising geopolitical and climate shocks could quickly tighten conditions; moderate urgency.

economic.acceleration.note: Structural vulnerabilities like high debt and leverage are building slowly, indicating steady but not explosive acceleration.

economic.interdependence.note: Global financial integration means shocks quickly propagate; economic distress is a central node in the risk network, coupling with debt, trade, and geopolitics.

economic.irreversibility.source: World Bank GEP, long-term growth scarring
economic.irreversibility.note: Crises leave persistent output and employment scars, but economies generally recover over a decade; partial irreversibility.

economic.gov_failure.note: Policymakers face difficult trade-offs; fiscal space limited, regulatory gaps remain; governance failure could amplify the next crisis.

economic.growth_rate.source: Expert judgment based on financial fragility indices
economic.growth_rate.note: No single clear quantitative proxy; expert judgment sets raw growth ~0.015/yr; log1p(0.015)*1.0=0.0149, capped at 0.03.
economic.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.015; raw=0.015, conversion 1.0, cap 0.03.

economic.threshold.source: Expert judgment on global financial system tipping point
economic.threshold.note: Threshold for a cascading global financial meltdown exceeds typical recessions but is below nuclear war; anchored to 2008 crisis severity.

epistemic.scale.note: Low trust in news, widespread misinformation, and AI-generated disinformation threaten informed public discourse on a global scale.

epistemic.urgency.note: Trust in institutions near historic lows; AI exacerbates disinformation; urgent countermeasures needed to protect democratic processes.

epistemic.acceleration.note: AI-generated content and organized disinformation campaigns are proliferating rapidly, with sharp increases in just a few years.

epistemic.interdependence.source: Nature Human Behaviour, misinformation and polarization, 2023
epistemic.interdependence.note: Epistemic breakdown fuels polarization, democratic backsliding, and reduces collective ability to address other systemic risks.

epistemic.irreversibility.note: Misinformation can be sticky, but societal trust can be rebuilt over time with sustained effort, so irreversibility is moderate.

epistemic.gov_failure.note: Some governments actively spread disinformation while regulation lags; probability of governance failure to maintain a healthy information ecosystem is high.

epistemic.growth_rate.source: Oxford Internet Institute, countries with organized manipulation 2020–2023
epistemic.growth_rate.note: Countries with disinformation campaigns rose ~15% per year; raw=0.15; log1p(0.15)*0.2=0.0279, rounded up to 0.029; cap 0.04.
epistemic.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.029; raw=0.15, conversion 0.2, cap 0.04.

epistemic.threshold.note: Threshold where societal consensus on facts and reality breaks down, undermining all collective responses to other systemic risks.

fragmentation_gov.scale.note: Multilateral system is struggling to address crises; fragmentation reduces global capacity to manage all other systemic threats.

fragmentation_gov.urgency.note: Deadlock on major conflicts and increasing veto use highlight immediate governance paralysis.

fragmentation_gov.acceleration.note: Great-power competition and bloc formation have intensified recently, accelerating institutional fragmentation.

fragmentation_gov.interdependence.note: Fragmentation directly undermines collective action on climate, pandemics, arms control, and trade, thus heavily interdependent.

fragmentation_gov.irreversibility.note: Rebuilding cooperative governance after deep fragmentation is difficult and slow, but historical precedents of renewal exist.

fragmentation_gov.gov_failure.source: UN Our Common Agenda and related assessments
fragmentation_gov.gov_failure.note: This threat is governance failure itself; the system's inability to reform is the core problem, hence almost maximal score.

fragmentation_gov.growth_rate.note: Veto use increased from 4 to 8 in recent years; raw growth proxy ~0.4/yr; log1p(0.4)*0.1=0.0336, capped at 0.04.
fragmentation_gov.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.034; raw=0.4, conversion 0.1, cap 0.04.

fragmentation_gov.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to UN and Munich Security Conference
fragmentation_gov.threshold.note: Threshold where global governance collapse becomes a self-reinforcing trap, making it impossible to address any other existential threat.

geopolitics.scale.note: Record high military spending and active conflicts; great-power conflict risks global economic and humanitarian catastrophe.

geopolitics.urgency.note: Sharp rise in spending and active hot wars indicate that escalation pressures are acute and demand immediate diplomatic attention.

geopolitics.acceleration.note: Spending and conflict counts are rising rapidly; the post-Cold War peace dividend has reversed, suggesting strong acceleration.

geopolitics.interdependence.note: Geopolitical rivalries block cooperation on climate, health, and nuclear risks, making them a central amplifying threat.

geopolitics.irreversibility.note: Once large-scale wars start, they tend to persist for years; recovery of cooperative relations is slow, but not impossible.

geopolitics.gov_failure.note: The inability of existing institutions to prevent or resolve conflicts, and the erosion of arms control, signify high governance failure.

geopolitics.growth_rate.note: Raw spending growth ~0.08/yr; log1p(0.08)*0.55=0.0423, capped at 0.045, effectively capped at 0.045 for mu.
geopolitics.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.042; raw=0.08, conversion 0.55, cap 0.045.

geopolitics.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to SIPRI and Munich Security
geopolitics.threshold.note: Threshold for great-power war with global consequences; slightly below nuclear threshold because conventional escalation could precede nuclear use.

minerals.scale.note: High concentration of clean-energy mineral supply chains poses risk to energy transition and economic stability globally.

minerals.urgency.note: Demand for lithium, cobalt, etc. surging; bottlenecks could stall decarbonization this decade unless addressed.

minerals.acceleration.note: Lithium demand tripled, cobalt up 70% in 5 years; acceleration is rapid as clean energy deployment scales.

minerals.interdependence.note: Supply chain disruptions affect energy, defense, and technology sectors; tightly coupled with geopolitics and trade.

minerals.irreversibility.source: World Bank, Minerals for Climate Action, 2020
minerals.irreversibility.note: Short-term bottlenecks can be overcome by investment and substitution, but environmental damage from mining can be lasting.

minerals.gov_failure.source: EU Critical Raw Materials Act analysis, 2023
minerals.gov_failure.note: Policy efforts are nascent; high concentration and geopolitical weaponization risk indicate moderate governance failure likelihood.

minerals.growth_rate.source: IEA critical minerals market doubling 2017–2022, CAGR ~15%
minerals.growth_rate.note: Raw market growth ~0.15/yr; log1p(0.15)*0.22=0.0307, capped at 0.04.
minerals.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.031; raw=0.15, conversion 0.22, cap 0.04.

minerals.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on IEA and USGS
minerals.threshold.note: Threshold where mineral supply constraints severely disrupt global energy transition and economic stability.

nuclear.scale.source: Robock et al., Nuclear winter, 2007, & modern analyses
nuclear.scale.note: Even a limited nuclear war could cause global famine and climate disruption; scale is near-absolute in worst case.

nuclear.urgency.source: Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, Doomsday Clock 2024
nuclear.urgency.note: Rhetoric and modernization trends raise risk; clock at 90 seconds to midnight underscores extreme urgency.

nuclear.acceleration.note: Modernization programs are accelerating, and deployed warhead numbers may be increasing after a long decline.

nuclear.interdependence.source: SIPRI report on nuclear and cyber/AI nexus, 2022
nuclear.interdependence.note: Nuclear risks are increasingly entangled with cyber threats, AI, and geopolitics; an incident in one domain could spiral.

nuclear.irreversibility.note: Nuclear war's effects on climate, agriculture, and civilization would be effectively irreversible on human timescales.

nuclear.gov_failure.source: Arms control erosion (INF, Open Skies, etc.)
nuclear.gov_failure.note: Collapse of key treaties, lack of new agreements, and rhetoric suggest governance failure is already advanced.

nuclear.growth_rate.note: Usable stockpiles are creeping upward; raw growth proxy ~0.018/yr; log1p(0.018)*0.9=0.0161, capped at 0.035.
nuclear.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.016; raw=0.018, conversion 0.9, cap 0.035.

nuclear.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to nuclear war consequences
nuclear.threshold.note: Highest threshold on the dashboard, reflecting that nuclear war is the ultimate systemic catastrophe; slightly above climate due to sudden onset.

oceans.scale.note: Ocean warming, acidification, deoxygenation, and overfishing threaten marine ecosystems and the billions who depend on them.

oceans.urgency.source: UNESCO State of the Ocean Report 2022
oceans.urgency.note: Multiple stressors are already causing severe impacts; urgent action needed to curb overfishing and reduce emissions.

oceans.acceleration.source: IPCC SROCC, ocean heat and acidification trends
oceans.acceleration.note: Ocean heat content and acidification rates are accelerating, but regional fisheries management can slow some declines.

oceans.interdependence.note: Oceans regulate climate, provide food, and support biodiversity; degradation interacts with all planetary boundaries.

oceans.irreversibility.note: Many ocean changes are irreversible for centuries; overfishing may be partially reversible but can cause permanent ecosystem shifts.

oceans.gov_failure.note: Overfishing persists despite regional management; high seas governance fragmented; governance response insufficient.

oceans.growth_rate.source: Composite: FAO fish stock status, IPCC acidification, coral bleaching trends
oceans.growth_rate.note: Composite degradation pressure proxy raw=0.012/yr; log1p(0.012)*1.0=0.0119, capped at 0.03.
oceans.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.012; raw=0.012, conversion 1.0, cap 0.03.

oceans.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to SROCC and FAO
oceans.threshold.note: Threshold for widespread marine ecosystem collapse, including functional extinction of major fish stocks and coral reef systems.

pandemics.scale.source: Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness, May 2021
pandemics.scale.note: COVID-19 demonstrated global health, economic, and social devastation; a future pandemic could be worse.

pandemics.urgency.note: Global preparedness remains inadequate; reforms are slow, and the next pandemic could emerge at any time.

pandemics.acceleration.source: Plowright et al., Land use-induced spillover, 2021
pandemics.acceleration.note: Spillover events are increasing due to deforestation, wildlife trade, and climate change; acceleration is clear.

pandemics.interdependence.note: A pandemic triggers cascading failures in health, supply chains, finance, and governance simultaneously.

pandemics.irreversibility.note: Economic and social systems can rebound, but deaths and long-term health impacts are irreversible; overall moderate.

pandemics.gov_failure.note: National and global responses failed at every stage; reforms have been insufficient, suggesting high probability of repeat failure.

pandemics.growth_rate.source: Marani et al., historical spillover frequency, BMJ 2023
pandemics.growth_rate.note: Outbreak frequency rising ~5%/yr; raw=0.05; log1p(0.05)*0.9=0.0439, capped at 0.05.
pandemics.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.044; raw=0.05, conversion 0.9, cap 0.05.

pandemics.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to COVID-19 and engineered pathogen risks
pandemics.threshold.note: Threshold for a pandemic that overwhelms global health systems and causes severe societal disruption; higher than natural COVID-19 but below nuclear.

pollution.scale.source: Lancet Commission on pollution and health, 2022
pollution.scale.note: 9 million premature deaths annually, with impacts across air, water, chemicals; scale is immense and global.

pollution.urgency.note: Chemical production doubling by 2030; deaths rising; urgent action needed but regulatory frameworks exist, so urgency moderate-high.

pollution.acceleration.source: UNEP GCO II, chemical industry CAGR 4%
pollution.acceleration.note: Production and waste are growing steadily; acceleration is evident but offset by some regional improvements.

pollution.interdependence.note: Pollution interacts with climate, biodiversity, and health systems; a classic systemic threat.

pollution.irreversibility.note: PFAS and other persistent pollutants last centuries; some air and water pollution can be cleaned relatively quickly, so blend of high and moderate.

pollution.gov_failure.note: Despite scientific consensus, deaths haven't declined; many countries lack adequate chemical regulation, indicating governance gap.

pollution.growth_rate.source: UNEP GCO II, chemical production doubling 2000–2017, CAGR ~4%
pollution.growth_rate.note: Raw production growth ~0.04/yr; log1p(0.04)*0.7=0.0275, capped at 0.04.
pollution.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.0275; raw=0.04, conversion 0.7, cap 0.04.

pollution.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to Lancet and planetary boundaries
pollution.threshold.note: Threshold where chemical pollution and waste cause widespread ecosystem and health collapse, but partly reversible with massive cleanup.

soils.scale.note: Up to 40% of land degraded, affecting food security, water, and climate; scale is global and threatening.

soils.urgency.note: Already affecting billions; business-as-usual will worsen crisis, but solutions exist, tempering extreme urgency.

soils.acceleration.note: Area of degraded land increasing steadily; not explosive, but consistent acceleration.

soils.interdependence.note: Soils link food, water, climate, biodiversity; their degradation ripples across all these domains.

soils.irreversibility.note: Some soils can recover with restoration, but desertification and erosion can be effectively permanent on human timescales.

soils.gov_failure.note: Restoration pledges cover only a fraction of degraded land; governance and investment remain insufficient.

soils.growth_rate.source: UNCCD technical brief, degraded land expansion ~0.9%/yr
soils.growth_rate.note: Annual expansion of degraded area relative to current base ~0.009/yr; log1p(0.009)*1.0=0.00897, capped at 0.025.
soils.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.009; raw=0.009, conversion 1.0, cap 0.025.

soils.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to UNCCD and IPBES
soils.threshold.note: Threshold where soil degradation triggers widespread food system collapse and forced migration.

space.scale.note: Debris congestion threatens key orbits; a Kessler syndrome could deny satellite services globally, affecting communications, weather, and navigation.

space.urgency.source: Secure World Foundation Global Counterspace Capabilities 2023
space.urgency.note: Anti-satellite tests and rapid orbit filling raise immediate risk of collisions; urgent mitigation needed.

space.acceleration.source: Space Foundation The Space Report 2023 Q4
space.acceleration.note: Launch rates and debris counts increasing sharply; acceleration is very high as commercial constellations deploy.

space.interdependence.note: Space services underpin modern economy, defense, and science; failure would cascade globally, hence maximum coupling.

space.irreversibility.source: ESA Space Debris FAQ, Kessler syndrome analysis
space.irreversibility.note: A runaway debris cascade could make orbits unusable for generations; effectively irreversible on human timescales.

space.gov_failure.source: UN COPUOS debris mitigation guidelines, non-binding
space.gov_failure.note: Existing guidelines are voluntary; rapid commercial expansion outpaces regulation; governance gap is severe.

space.growth_rate.note: Tracked object population growing ~20%/yr; raw=0.2; log1p(0.2)*0.18=0.0328, capped at 0.04.
space.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.033; raw=0.2, conversion 0.18, cap 0.04.

space.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on ESA and OECD
space.threshold.note: Threshold for a Kessler syndrome onset making LEO unusable, with severe global knock-on effects.

supply.scale.source: World Bank LPI 2023, OECD trade resilience reports
supply.scale.note: Supply chains have shown resilience but face growing disruptions from climate, geopolitics, and policy; scale is global but not yet catastrophic.

supply.urgency.source: OECD International trade in the wake of multiple shocks, 2023
supply.urgency.note: Recent shocks highlight fragility; urgency to build resilience is high as trade restrictions rise.

supply.acceleration.source: IMF Working Paper on supply chain pressures 2023
supply.acceleration.note: Pandemic-era pressures have eased, but structural risks are building slowly; acceleration is modest.

supply.interdependence.note: Interconnected global value chains mean local disruptions cascade; supply chains are a backbone of economic system.

supply.irreversibility.note: Firms can adapt sourcing over time; but infrastructure damage from climate may lock in some fragilities permanently.

supply.gov_failure.note: Policy responses are mixed: some invest in resilience, others impose export controls that weaken the system.

supply.growth_rate.source: OECD trade restrictive measures covering ~9% of imports, up from 1%
supply.growth_rate.note: Trade restriction proxy growing ~12%/yr; raw=0.12; log1p(0.12)*0.25=0.0283, capped at 0.04.
supply.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.028; raw=0.12, conversion 0.25, cap 0.04.

supply.threshold.source: Expert judgment based on World Bank and OECD
supply.threshold.note: Threshold where cascading supply chain failures cause global shortages and economic paralysis.

water.scale.note: Half the global population faces severe water scarcity at least part of the year; water stress is already a civilizational-scale challenge.

water.urgency.source: UN WWDR 2023, WMO State of Global Water Resources 2022
water.urgency.note: Crisis is now; 2.2 billion lack safe drinking water; urgent investment and governance reform needed this decade.

water.acceleration.source: WMO State of Global Water Resources 2022, trends
water.acceleration.note: Climate change intensifies hydrological cycle; droughts and floods increasing, but variability still high.

water.interdependence.source: Global Commission on the Economics of Water 2023
water.interdependence.note: Water links climate, food, energy, health, and peace; it is a central nexus threat.

water.irreversibility.source: IPCC AR6 WG II, water chapter
water.irreversibility.note: Aquifer depletion can be permanent; glaciers melting irreversibly; some surface water systems may recover if managed.

water.gov_failure.note: Despite decades of commitments, billions lack safe water; governance and financing gaps persist globally.

water.growth_rate.source: Kummu et al., water scarcity exposure growth, 2016
water.growth_rate.note: Population under scarcity growing ~2.8%/yr historically; raw=0.0276; log1p(0.0276)*0.9=0.0245, capped at 0.035.
water.growth_rate.calibration_note: Effective growth mu=0.0245; raw=0.0276, conversion 0.9, cap 0.035.

water.threshold.source: Expert judgment anchored to WWDR and WMO
water.threshold.note: Threshold where water scarcity and extreme events trigger widespread food and energy system failures.
